title: Beloved, not far (7:4)
hookLine: someone returning shouldn't think they're far from the righteous; they are beloved
tomorrow: peace to the far and the near. but who's the far one?

lines: A BROKEN STREAK. BACK TO ZERO.
cards: Miss a month at the gym and the app greets you with a broken streak and a sad little zero. Plenty of systems work that way: mess up, go to the back of the line. So here's an odd line from a law book.
Maimonides writes that someone who returns shouldn't think they're far from the righteous because of what they did.

Then he goes further, and quotes the sages: in the place where those who return stand, the completely righteous cannot stand. The person with the past stands somewhere the spotless person can't. How does that add up?

teach.b: Start with the first half, because it answers the back-of-the-line worry.
The one who does teshuvah, who returns, Maimonides says, is beloved and desired before the Creator, as if they had never sinned. Beloved. In Hebrew, ahuv.
Not tolerated, not on probation. The streak doesn't reset to zero; the zero is gone. Now the puzzle.
Why would the returner stand higher than someone who never slipped? His answer is one sentence.

teach.h: THEY TASTED IT AND LEFT IT.
teach.b: They tasted the wrong, and they left it, and they overpowered their own pull toward it. The person who was never drawn to that thing didn't have to win that fight. The returner did.
So the place they stand isn't a prize for the mess. It's for the turning, real effort made against something that already had a grip.
Here's a line to say out loud tonight: in this book, a past isn't a debt that keeps you at the back. It's the hill you climbed. One honest guardrail.
Maimonides isn't saying go get a past so you can climb it.
Earlier in these same laws, he lists sinning with a plan to return later as something that blocks return.
The point isn't the fall. The point is that the one who got up is not far.

how: Jewish communities often honor a ba'al teshuvah, someone who has returned to observance or turned from a wrong, and the saying about where returners stand is widely quoted when they're welcomed.

o: forgiven by God, but still kept a little way off
loved and wanted by God, not kept at a distance
admired by others once their past is forgotten

p: beloved, as if they'd never sinned
they tasted the wrong and left it
never had that fight to win

s: someone who returns starts over at the back of the line
Maimonides: they shouldn't think they're far. they're beloved, as if they'd never sinned.
Maimonides says to sin first, so you can return and climb higher
the same laws list sinning with a plan to return as a block to return.
the sages say returners stand where the completely righteous can't
Maimonides quotes it and gives the reason: they overpowered a pull that already had a grip.

games.q: your cousin has been sober for two years. at dinner an uncle says, 'well, he's no saint like his brother.' what would 7:4 say to the uncle?
o: he's right; the brother never slipped, so he's ahead.
they're simply equal now; the past cancels out.
he isn't far; he won a fight his brother never had.
games.why: 'as if he'd never sinned' is only the first half. the second: where returners stand, the completely righteous can't, because the returner overpowered a real pull.

practice: Say one short sentence out loud, quietly if others are near: i am not far. Say it slowly, and then once more, a little slower. Notice whatever in you argues back, and let it talk without answering it.
Then rest in the quiet that's left.

wordCard.voice: Beloved: ahuv in Hebrew. Maimonides' word for the one who returns: beloved and desired, as if they'd never sinned.

orig.note: Hebrew: beloved. Maimonides pairs it with nechmad, desired.

carryVoice: Your line: beloved, not far. A past is the hill you climbed, not the back of the line. Nineteen of thirty in the laws of return.

sources.ref: Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 7:4 (the returner is beloved and desired as if they never sinned; they tasted sin and left it; where returners stand the completely righteous cannot)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (where returners stand, the completely righteous cannot stand)
Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 4:1 (one who says 'I will sin and then return' is among those blocked from return)
